definition: Blandish means to coax someone by flattering them.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word blandish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know blandish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The nephew blandished his aunt through every visit — her roses, her pastry, her violin — and drove home each time in her car.
Praise is the mildest rung and may be completely deserved — praising a speech asks for nothing back, while blandishing always does.
Flatter stops short of blandish: flattery merely overdoes the compliments, but blandishment aims them — the praise is a doorbell rung just before a request.

To butter someone up is the playground version of blandishing — praise laid on thick right before a favor, so obvious that everyone within earshot knows it. Blandish is the courtly, bookish cousin: the same flattery-for-a-purpose, applied so smoothly the target may never notice the lever.

To wheedle is to get your way by sweet, whiny persistence — pleading and pleading until the other person gives in just to end it. Blandish never begs: it works through praise, warming the target with compliments so that the request, when it finally comes, is hard to refuse.

Every restaurant in the city feared Renata Voss, whose reviews could empty a dining room by Friday.
The chef at Marlow's never sent free dishes — she would have flagged that in print.
Instead he learned what she loved outside the job: obscure jazz pressings, hand-thrown pottery.
When she dined, he found ways to blandish her without a single word about food — a passing compliment on her essay about Coltrane, a question about her kiln, always brief, always sincere-sounding.
Colleagues assumed the warm review that followed was luck.
Voss herself never connected the stars she awarded to those easy little conversations.
That was the measure of his skill: the flattery worked best on the one person trained to detect it.
